title: Where does K appear?
hook: Are words beginning with K easier to find than words with K third?

knows: basic arithmetic and reading a small table
doesNotKnow: Separate ease of retrieval from the frequency of the underlying class.

misconception: The quantities in this case can be combined without checking their reference, denominator, or information boundary.
objective: Separate ease of retrieval from the frequency of the underlying class.
keyState: Both complete computed cases are visible as retained observations; the question-case picture survives Reset.

claims.text: A toy list contains two words starting with K and four with K third. What is the true first-to-third count ratio? Toy inputs A=[2, 4, 2.5, 1]; B=[2, 4, 1, 1].
claims.source: Local explicit hypothetical assumptions in spec.ts and model.ts; not participant measurements.

claims.text: Computed results: [[5, 4, 0.5], [2, 4, 0.5]]. Labels: First retrieval, Third retrieval, Count ratio.
claims.source: compute() in the lesson-local model.ts; finite numeric operations over the explicit inputs.

claims.text: Retrieval salience can rank classes differently from their actual counts in this toy rule. Removing that unequal salience restores the frequency ranking. Ease of recall is therefore a possible input to judgment, not a count of the population.
claims.source: The two controlled cases in spec.ts; scope limited to these toy inputs and displayed model rule.

claims.text: A new toy case uses K first count=2, K third count=4, First salience=1, Third salience=1. What is Count ratio? Answer: 0.5.
claims.source: compute() applied to the contrasting new input case; source list is an idea pointer only.

recall.question: A new toy case uses K first count=2, K third count=4, First salience=1, Third salience=1. What is Count ratio?
recall.why: Applying the stated toy rule to the new inputs gives 0.5. The result depends on these assumptions; it is not a universal behavioral response.

sourceProvenance.text: People think more words start with K than have K third, because first letters are easier to recall; the reverse is true (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973).
sourceProvenance.caveat: Original list says figures are approximate and papers were not individually rechecked. No empirical source is verified by this build.

meaningfulDifference: Separate ease of retrieval from the frequency of the underlying class.
